![The Self-Refine loop: an initial output from model $M$ is sent back to the same $M$ for feedback, then $M$ uses that feedback to produce a refined output, with the feedback-refine cycle repeating until a stopping condition is met. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

In *Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback* [[1]](#ref-1) ([NeurIPS 2023](https://neurips.cc/)), [Aman Madaan](https://madaan.github.io/), [Niket Tandon](https://niket.tandon.info/), and collaborators at [CMU](https://www.cmu.edu/), [Allen Institute for AI](https://allenai.org/), [University of Washington](https://www.washington.edu/), [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/), [UC San Diego](https://ucsd.edu/), and [Google Research](https://research.google/) show that a single frozen large language model (LLM) can act as generator, critic, and rewriter in a prompt-only loop, and that this loop improves outputs across seven generation tasks without any additional training.

> Like humans, large language models (LLMs) do not always generate the best output on their first try. Motivated by how humans refine their written text, we introduce *Self-Refine*, an approach for improving initial outputs from LLMs through iterative feedback and refinement. The main idea is to generate an initial output using an LLMs; then, the same LLMs provides feedback for its output and uses it to refine itself, iteratively. Self-Refine *does not require any supervised training data, additional training, or reinforcement learning*, and instead *uses a single LLM as the generator, refiner, and feedback provider*. We evaluate Self-Refine across 7 diverse tasks, ranging from dialog response generation to mathematical reasoning, using state-of-the-art (GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, and GPT-4) LLMs. Across all evaluated tasks, outputs generated with Self-Refine are preferred by humans and automatic metrics over those generated with the same LLM using conventional one-step generation, *improving by ~20% absolute on average in task performance*. Our work demonstrates that *even state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-4 can be further improved at test time* using our simple, standalone approach.

## Methods

The method is deliberately minimal. Self-Refine takes an input $x$, uses three handcrafted few-shot prompts — `p_gen`, `p_fb`, `p_refine` — and runs the same model $M$ three ways: $M(p_{\text{gen}} \Vert x)$ produces the initial output $y_0$; $M(p_{\text{fb}} \Vert x \Vert y_t)$ emits natural-language feedback on $y_t$; and the refine step writes $y_{t+1}$ from the model conditioned on the input plus the full history of prior outputs and feedback ($y_0, fb_0, \ldots, y_t, fb_t$). No fine-tuning, no external reward model, no reinforcement learning. The loop halts either at a fixed iteration budget or when $M$ itself signals that no further refinement is needed. The paper evaluates on dialogue response generation, code optimization, code readability improvement, mathematical reasoning (GSM8K [[5]](#ref-5)), sentiment reversal, acronym generation, and constrained generation, with base models GPT-3.5 (`text-davinci-003` and `gpt-3.5-turbo`), [ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/), Codex [[6]](#ref-6) (`code-davinci-002`), and [GPT-4](https://openai.com/index/gpt-4/).

Two things distinguish the prompts from generic "what do you think?" critique prompting. First, `p_fb` is few-shot-exemplified to elicit feedback that is **actionable** (names a concrete change to make) and **specific** (pinpoints the exact phrase or line to change). The Figure 2(e) example — "This code is slow as it uses a for loop... A better approach is to use the formula `(n(n+1))/2`" — is the template: identify the offending construct, propose the replacement. Second, `p_refine` is also few-shot, with $\langle x, y_t, fb_t, y_{t+1} \rangle$ quadruples that show how to translate feedback into a concrete edit rather than paraphrase or hedge.

The few-shot exemplars in `p_fb` are themselves built from a per-task **rubric** — 10 qualitative aspects for Dialogue Response Generation (relevant, informative, interesting, consistent, etc.), a 5-dimension rubric for Acronym Generation (pronunciation, spelling, etc.), the missing-concept checklist for Constrained Generation. The rubric is never invoked explicitly at inference. The model learns it from the exemplars.

The top row illustrates dialogue generation, where an initial response gets transformed into a more engaging one that also addresses the user's intent. The bottom row illustrates code optimization, where a brute-force loop is replaced with the closed-form $n(n+1)/2$. ## Results

Across the seven tasks, Self-Refine beats single-shot prompting by 5–40 points absolute, averaging around 20 points of improvement by human preference and automatic metrics. The gains are largest on tasks with multifaceted or hard-to-define objectives (dialogue, code readability, constrained generation) and smallest on math reasoning, where Table 1 shows essentially no improvement (↑0 to ↑0.2) — the paper attributes this to the feedback model's inability to detect subtle math errors. Code optimization improves by 8.7 points absolute on GPT-4 (27.3 → 36.0), and by up to 13 points absolute when applied to Codex. Human raters prefer Self-Refine outputs at rates generally consistent with the automatic metrics. The paper releases prompts and code.

![Self-Refine results on various tasks using GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, and GPT-4 as base LLM. Self-Refine consistently improves the base LLM across preference- and rule-based metrics, with the smallest gains on Math Reasoning. Table 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table1.png){fig-align="center"}

The paper also ablates the feedback prompt itself, replacing actionable+specific feedback with generic "what do you think?" feedback or no feedback at all (Table 2). The actionable+specific shape carries most of the signal, especially on tasks where "good output" is hard to define — Sentiment Reversal goes from 43.2 to 31.2 to 0 across the three feedback regimes. On Code Optimization, where "fast" is well-defined, generic feedback already gets you most of the way there.

![Ablating the feedback prompt: Self-Refine's actionable+specific feedback vs. generic feedback ("Improve the efficiency of the code") vs. no feedback (the model still iterates but isn't explicitly given feedback). The gap is widest on Sentiment Reversal, where output quality is hardest to define from a one-line critique. Table 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table2.png){fig-align="center"}

## My Notes

- **The gain doesn't generalize beyond strong critics.** The ~20-point headline held up in the paper's own benchmarks but is sensitive to task and model. Kamoi et al. [[4]](#ref-4) [[4]](#ref-4)'s survey concludes that no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback generated by LLMs prompting themselves under fair settings, and they specifically flag Self-Refine's evaluation as over-stating the gain (Table 4 of the survey: weak prompts on the initial-response side combined with appropriate prompts on the self-correction side). On reasoning tasks, Huang et al. [[2]](#ref-2) [[2]](#ref-2) show intrinsic self-correction can degrade accuracy on average — Table 1's near-zero math result here was already a tell. The loop assumes the critic produces actionable feedback. When the critic is weak (smaller models make this worse rather than introduce it), the iterations don't help.
- **Feedback quality drives more gain than iteration count.** The paper omits the cleanest ablation: a single-pass critique-and-refine prompt that gives the base LLM the rubric without iteration. Without it, a substantial part of the gain on dialogue and constrained generation may be attributable to the rubric embedded in the feedback prompt rather than to iteration itself. [Reflexion](/posts/20260516-reflexion/) [[3]](#ref-3), which appeared around the same time, makes the memory question explicit: it persists verbal reflections across episodes, while Self-Refine's history is scoped to a single input.
- **The prompt-only antecedent of o1.** Self-Refine spends several times more tokens per problem than one-shot generation in exchange for task-quality gains — the same compute-for-quality tradeoff that [o1](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)-style models would later formalize with RL-trained chains, but realized through prompting alone. In 2023 the framing was novel. The *test-time compute* idiom only entered general usage with the o1 release in late 2024.
